items.title: Music-based interventions for anxiety and depression in adult cancer patients: an umbrella review of the evidence landscape and methodological quality.
items.venue: Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer

ai.headline: Music-based approaches may ease anxiety and depression in adults with cancer, but the evidence quality is weak.
ai.summary: This umbrella review examined 20 systematic reviews of trials testing music-based interventions for anxiety and depression in adults with cancer. Most reviews reported beneficial effects, but most were rated low or critically low in confidence, and many had a high risk of bias.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that while music might help people with cancer feel better, the current research is not strong enough to be certain.
ai.life_skill: Try listening to calming music if you feel anxious or low, but speak to a qualified healthcare professional about proven support options.
ai.fact: Music-based interventions are being studied as complementary approaches for managing anxiety and depression in adults with cancer.

quiz.answer: Confidence was constrained by limitations in methodological quality and reporting of existing systematic reviews.

ai.caveat: This is an umbrella review of systematic reviews, most of which were rated low or critically low in confidence and many had a high risk of bias, so the findings are not proof.

items.title: Does CBT change the brain? A systematic review of neuroimaging RCTs on anxiety disorders, depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder

ai.headline: CBT may change brain activity and connections linked to anxiety, depression and OCD, but evidence is early.
ai.summary: This systematic review looked at 17 randomised trials of cognitive behavioural therapy in adults with anxiety disorders, depression or OCD that used brain scans before and after treatment. It found changes in areas involved in emotional reactivity, control systems and their connections, with different patterns for each condition, though brain changes did not always line up with symptom improvement.
ai.why_it_matters: It suggests talking therapy can have measurable effects on the brain, helping us understand how psychological treatment works beyond just talking.
ai.life_skill: Notice how your thoughts and reactions shift after practising a new coping skill, rather than expecting immediate change.
ai.fact: CBT is linked to changes in brain regions involved in emotional reactivity, control and connectivity in anxiety disorders, depression and OCD.

quiz.question: Did brain changes always happen at the same time as symptom improvement in the reviewed trials?
quiz.answer: No, neural and clinical change did not always coincide.

ai.caveat: It is a preprint not yet peer reviewed, includes small samples and heterogeneous protocols, and five studies were at high risk of bias.

ai.summary: A systematic review of 174 studies over thirty years found that most used cross-sectional designs and non-probabilistic sampling, with only six randomised trials. ai.why_it_matters: It shows that claims about the practical usefulness of this diagnostic system rest mostly on observational evidence, not proof that it improves decisions or treatment results.

ai.fact: Only six of the 174 studies reviewed were randomised clinical trials.

quiz.answer: Cross-sectional designs were most common, used in 116 of the 174 studies.

ai.caveat: The review summarises existing studies, most of which were observational and cannot prove cause and effect.

ai.headline: AI-assisted systematic reviews scored lower on method quality and reporting than reviews without reported AI use.
ai.summary: Researchers compared 77 health systematic reviews that reported using AI with 154 matched reviews that did not. AI-assisted reviews had lower methodological-adherence scores and less complete reporting, though more were rated low risk of bias.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that AI tools in health evidence reviews may need careful human checking and transparency before the results are trusted for decisions.
ai.life_skill: Check whether a health review says how AI was used and whether humans verified the results before relying on it.
ai.fact: Among AI-assisted reviews, only 9.1% reported data-governance or ethics considerations.

quiz.question: Did AI-assisted reviews score higher or lower on the methodological-adherence measure than reviews with no reported AI use?
quiz.answer: AI-assisted reviews scored lower on average (7.58 versus 9.63).

ai.caveat: This is a preprint, not yet peer reviewed, and an observational matched study, so it cannot prove AI caused the lower scores.

quiz.answer: They propose sleep is a repair operator that reverses daily changes in brain energy and synaptic state, rather than only being a symptom or risk factor.

items.title: Doing Better at Doing Good: Lessons from a Bayesian Meta-Analysis After 20 Years of Poverty Graduation Programs -- by Samantha Carter, Edward Jee, Dean Karlan, Patrick Premand

ai.headline: Poverty graduation programmes raise income, consumption and wellbeing, and newer ones give better value for money.
ai.summary: Researchers analysed 49 studies of programmes that combine at least three of five parts: consumption support, savings help, skills training, coaching and a lump-sum cash transfer. On average, monthly consumption rose by 38 USD PPP (11%) and income by 28 USD PPP (15%), with gains also seen in savings, assets, food security, mental health and women’s empowerment. Programmes run from 2016 onward had much higher benefit-cost ratios (5.39) than earlier ones (2.89), though the reason for this improvement is not yet clear.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how anti-poverty programmes have improved over time and which design choices—such as transfer size and cost—matter most for getting good results.
ai.life_skill: Notice whether a programme’s benefits are large enough to justify its cost before supporting or joining it.
ai.fact: Programmes with transfers of at least 400 USD PPP had larger effects but were not more cost-effective than smaller-transfer programmes.

quiz.question: What happened to benefit-cost ratios for poverty graduation programmes implemented from 2016 onward compared with earlier programmes?
quiz.answer: They rose from 2.89 through 2015 to 5.39 from 2016 onward.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, and it cannot prove that newer programme designs caused the better results.

ai.life_skill: Notice when an AI gives different answers to the same question and treat less consistent answers with caution.
ai.fact: Self-generated labels used to adapt AI models can contain errors from majority bias and limited sampling variation.

quiz.answer: They proposed Prompt-Conditional Distributionally Robust DPO, which makes updates from uncertain prompts more conservative.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, so its findings are not yet confirmed.
